Role of public and private sectors in power generation and distribution 
 *283. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
  DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
 Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether, emphasizing the increased role for the public sector in power generation and the 
private sector in the distribution business, he has decided to strengthen technological and managerial 
expertise of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in power sector and synergies their roles, to 
complement generation capacity building efforts; 
 (b) if so, what are the main suggestion s made to the PSUs in the power sector; 
 (c) how many of these suggestions have been considered by those PSUs; and 
 (d) to what extent the power generation target s would be achieved during the Eleventh Five 
Year Plan? 
 THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Power 
places emphasis on capacity building in power se ctor. With growing competition and restructuring of 
the sector, the focus is on reorienting and upgr ading managerial approach and improving work 
efficiency through structured skills upgradation and improvement programme. 
 The changes caused due to technological advan ces and upgradation are tackled through multi 
pronged strategy in the three ma jor areas in the Power Sector i.e. Generation, Transmission and 
Distribution. The major initiatives taken are as follows: 
 I. Cadre Development: 
  (i) Developing the cadre at induction leve l through institutionaliz ing career development 
programmes like B. Tech in Power through the National Power Training Institute 
(NPTI) for developing engineers specifically for the power sector. 

 8
   In addition, a distance l earning Advanced Certificate pr ogramme in Power Distribution 
Management has been initiated by Ministry of Power through the Indira Gandhi National 
Open University (IGNOU) to provide an overall perspectiv e on power distribution. The 
programme commenced in 2007 and has covere d more than 1500 participants. A six 
months Post Graduate Diploma is also offered by NPTI in Transmission and 
Distribution. 
  (ii) Building a skilled manpower pool to cove r new trades as well as upgrading the skills to 
cater to technological advances has been in itiated by the Ministry of Power through 
‘Adopt an ITI’ Scheme wherein the power developers and utilitie s are encouraged to 
adopt ITIs near the project areas. Some of  the Utilities that have adopted/built ITIs 
include NTPC 25 Nos., NHPC 6 Nos., DVC 8 Nos. and Tata Power 4 Nos. 
  (iii) Ministry of Power in collaboration with  IGNOU has recently launched a distance learning 
programme for Technicians in the Sector, delivered through multi media of print 
(course books), teleconfer encing and practicals. The programme will help the 
Technicians to upgrade their skills and provide them opport unity in career growth as 
certificate awarded by IGNOU will be equivalent  to that of ITI. It will also open new 
career stream for young students at entran ce level to pursue the programme with a 
ready placement potential. 
  (iv) To upgrade managerial skills and reorie nt the approach toward s sectoral changes, a 
post Graduate Energy Management program me has been institutionalized by the 
Ministry of Power through the Management Development Institute. The programme 
focuses on developing future leaders with particular emphasis on implementation of 
enactments relating to power distribution. 
 II. Induction level/ Refresher Programmes: 
  (i) All utilities in the Central Sector ha ve devised structured programmes catering to 
various levels. While in generation, NT PC, NHPC, THDC, SJVNL and NEEPCO have 
inhouse facilities along with in stitutional arrangements with other training institutes to 
cater to their training needs. The cove rage during 2006-07 to 2008-09 (to date) is: 
NIPC about 61,000 NHPC about 26,000, THDC about 2,800, SJVNL and NEEPCO 
about 1,835 trainees respectively. 
  (ii) In Transmission, Power Grid Corporatio n of India Ltd. (PGCIL) has adequate training 
structure to implement vari ous programmes. The covera ge during 2006-07 to 2007-08 
is more than 8000 persons. 

 9
  (iii) In Distribution, the Ministry of Power has institutionalized a structured distribution 
related project, called the Distribution Reforms Upgrade Management (DRUM) 
Programme. The programme wa s initiated in 2005 with ta rgeted coverage of 20,000 
participants. More than 25, 000 participants have already been covered and an 
institutional network of 20 Inst itutions establishe d covering all regions of the country. 
The programme primarily encompasses shor t term programmes covering the core 
technical and management theme, relevant  to distribution business operation. 
Technological advances have also been addressed through programmes delivered by 
manufacturers on Metering technology and Di stribution system equipment to enable 
direct interface between manufacturers and users. The overall coverage through the 
Distribution Reform Upgrade Management programme is as under:

 (d) The Planning Commission had set a capacity addition target of 78,700 MW for the 11th Five

capacity realizable with close monitoring, as estima ted by the Central Electricity Authority during 11th

and 3,380 MW from Nuclear. A capacity of 11,322 MW has already been co mmissioned during 11th

Welfare of street children 
 *288. SHRI AMBETH RAJAN: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware that a large number of children in India, mostly in all the 
metropolitan cities, and particularly in Delhi, are st aying on the roadside and se lling things at the traffic 
signals; 
 (b) if so, what makes them to do so; 
 (c) whether any step was taken by Government for the betterment of those children;  
and 
 (d) if so, the details thereof? 

 12
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINI STRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) A large number of children in India are found 
staying of streets and roadside and selling things at traffic signals, specially in metro cities. There are 
several socio-economic factors for this which include poverty, illiteracy, migration and others. 
 (c) and (d) Several schemes and programmes are being implemented by the Government for 
betterment of such children. The following scheme s are being implemented by the Ministry of Women 
and Child Development: 
 (i) An Integrated Programme for Street Children: The scheme is implemented for providing 
non-institutional support neces sary for wholesome development of street children. Under 
the scheme, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are fu nded by the Ministry for 
providing facilities to street children which incl ude shelter, nutrition, health care, recreation, 
education (formal and non-formal), vocational tr aining etc. Childline service is also being 
provided under the scheme which is 24-hour toll free emergency phone outreach service for 
children in need of care and protection. Any ch ild/concerned adult on behalf of a child, can 
call 1098, and avail of the service at any time of  the day or night. Childline is available in 83 
cities in the country. 
 (ii) Scheme for Working Children in Need of Care and Protection: Under this scheme working 
children are provided non formal education and vo cational training to facilitate their entry/re-
entry into mainstream education with a view to preventing their future exploitation. 
 (iii) Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS): The Ministry has recently formulated a new 
centrally sponsored scheme, namely, the Integr ated Child Protection  Scheme (ICPS) for 
implementation during the 11th Plan Pe riod through the St ate Governments/UT 
Administrations with main obj ective of providing a safe an d secure environment to the 
children in need of care and protection. Unde r this scheme, provision has been made to 
cater to all children in need of care and protection particularly beggars, street children and 
working children, rag pickers, orphaned, tr afficked, run-away children and any other 
vulnerable group of children. However, this sc heme is yet to be approved by the competent 
authority.

 (a) whether Government has achieved the target  under the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran

 THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMA R SHINDE): (a) to (c) The Rajiv Gandhi 
Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY)  aims at electrification of 1, 15,000 un-electrified villages. The 
implementing agencies have reported that rural elec trification works have been carried out to electrify 
53,048 un-electrified villages and intensive electrification of 66,808 villages in the country under 
RGGVY as on 01.12.2008. 
 State-wise and year-wise progr ess of village electrification under RGGVY till September 2008 is

un-electrified villages as on 30th September 2008. They have also report ed that intensive electrification 
of 61,375 already electrified villages have been carried out under RGGVY as on 30th September 2008. 
 (d) The performance of RGGVY in some States has been slow because of the following 
reasons: 
  Delay in receipt of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). 
  Delay in finalization of BPL lists by some states. 
  Delay in forest clearance. 
  Delays in land acquisition for 33/11 KV sub-stations. 
  Limited number of good agencies availa ble for execution of turnkey contracts. 

 15
  Very high rates quoted by contracting agencies. 
  Shortage of material like poles etc. and high prices. 
  Delays in issuance of road pe rmit and way bills by the States. 
  Delays by State Utilities in taking over of ph ysical assets created by Central Power Sector 
Undertakings (CPSUs). 
  Delays in issuance of Panchayat Cert ificates for village electrification. 
  Lack of awareness among village rs for taking new connections. 
  Very poor upstream rural electric ity infrastructure in some states. 
  Delay or refusal to waive state and local  taxes on line materials by some states. 
  Difficult terrain in some states and floods. 
 (e) For effective implementation of RGGVY, the following steps have been taken: 
  Government of India has set up an inter-Mini sterial Monitoring Committee which periodically 
meets to sanction projects and review progress of implementation. 
  States have been advised to set up district  committees to monitor the progress of rural 
electrification works. Most of the states have notified formation of district committees. 
  The Government of India as also Rural Elect rification Corporation (REC), the nodal agency 
for RGGVY, conduct frequent review meetings  with all the stakeh olders; the concerned 
State Governments, state po wer utilities and implementing  agencies for expeditious 
implementation of the scheme on the agreed schedules. 
  For speedier and effective implementation of projects, their execution has been taken up on 
turnkey basis. 
  To ensure qualitative execution of rural electri fication works, a thr ee tier quality control 
mechanism has been enforced under RGGVY. 
  Grant amount of BPL connection has been  enhanced to Rs.2200/- from Rs. 1500/-. 
  To take care of the cost escalation, cost norm s for village electrificat ion have been revised 
upward. 
  National Workshop was organized in collabora tion with IEEMA to ensure timely supply of 
materials. 
  Fund flow has been streamlined by use of  e-transfer, to avoid parking of funds. 
 Chief Ministers and Chief Se cretaries of State Governments have been requested to 
constitute Coordination Committ ee under chairmanship of Chie f Secretary to address state 
level issues for expeditious implementation of the scheme.

  MS. SUSHILA TIRIYA:  
 Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that, in view of the in creasing number of court cases, the Chief Justice of 
India has also stressed the need to set up more  benches of Supreme Court and to increase the 
number of CBI courts, along with other courts; 
 (b) whether it is also a fact that the number of pending cases in family courts as well is

in the Judge strength of the Su preme Court from the present 25 to 30 Judges, excluding the Chief

have been instituted for speedy disposal of lo ng pending Sessions cases and the cases involving

Problems in power sector 
 *295. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
  SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:  
 Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether his Ministry has decided to have a meeting with the power project developers, in 
the wake of ongoing financial crisis; 
 (b) whether a Prime Minister’s panel has been set up to study the credit crunch in the power 
sector; 
 (c) whether the National Thermal Power Corporat ion (NTPC) is said to have achieved capacity 
addition target; 
 (d) whether Dabhol power output has fallen at 300 MW; 
 (e) if so, what were the main points suggested during the meeting; and 
 (f) what are the concrete measures taken by Government to help power projects to achieve 
their targets? 
 THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) An interactive stock-taking 
session with State Power Secretaries, Central Po wer Utilities, Fina ncial Institutions and private 
developers was organized by the Mi nistry of Power on 3rd December , 2008 on measures to accelerate 
the pace of setting up of power projects. 
 (b) No such panel has been formed in the Mini stry of Power. However, the views of the power 
sector have been placed before the appropriate forum. 
 (c) NTPC Ltd.’s capacity addition target of 20, 000 MW during the 11th Plan period is expected 
to be achieved. 
 (d) Currently, the output from Ratnagiri Gas and Power Private Limite d (RGPPL), Dabhol has 
reduced to 300-320 MW (approx.) on account of catastr ophic failure of Gas Turbines and preventive 
shutdown of other two running m achines on the advice of original equipment manufacturer, M/s. 
General Electric, USA. 

 23
 (e) The main recommendations emerging fr om the interactive session are as follows: 
 (i) The power sector is a basi c infrastructure requirement for the economy. It is a well  
regulated sector with good retu rns on investment. It is capita l intensive and hence requires 
adequate funding, needing an increase in exposure limits from banks and financial 
institutions. 
 (ii) Timely coal linkage is to be granted to  new power projects by holding regular and more 
frequent meetings of Standing Linkage Committee (Long-Term). 
 (iii) Natural gas may be made available to po wer projects on the highest priority to avoid 
standard/idle generating capacity. 
 (iv) Transmission tie-up is to be  arranged for private power projects. 
 (v) Ministry of Power may review and liberalise the procedure of granting Mega Status to power 
projects. 
 (vi) Land acquisition process and various st atutory clearances for power projects could be 
expedited. 
 (f) The following measures have been taken by the Government to help power projects to 
achieve their targets: 
 (i) Rigorous monitoring of ca pacity addition of the on-going power generation projects. 
 (ii) Sensitizing the industry to the needs of increasing manufacturing cap acity and widening the 
vendor base for Main Plant equipment and Bala nce of Plants like Coal Handling Plant, Ash 
Handling, Plant, Water Treatment Plant, etc., by  organizing internatio nal conclave, regional 
workshops, etc. 
 (iii) Development of extensive network of tran smission system commensur ate with the capacity 
addition programme. Addition of new inter-regional transm ission capacities through 
development of National Grid. 
 (iv) Ensuring availability of funds throug h Power Finance Corporation (PFC) and Rural 
Electrification Corporation (REC) so that viable projects are not hampered. 
 (v) Coordination with various agencies to ensure backward and forward linkages for the 
upcoming projects including fuel linkages and various statutory clearances. 
 (vi) Creation of Special Purpose Vehicles for ex pediting land acquisition,  water availability, coal 
block allotment and initiating environment clearance for Ultra Mega Power Projects.

 *296. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
  SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
 Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE  DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 

 24
 (a) whether the University Grants Commissi on (UGC) has asked all the universities and 
colleges in the country to have an internal assurance cell, to improv e the quality of higher education 
being imparted; 
 (b) if so, whether all the Central Universities an d colleges are monitored by the UGC, in so far as 
imparting of higher education is concerned; 
 (c) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (d) what other steps Government proposes to ta ke to improve standard of education in colleges 
and universities, in consultation with the State Governments? 
 THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOP MENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) All 
Universities and Colleges accredit ed by the National Assessment  and Accreditation Council are 
required to establish an Internal Quality Assurance Cell. An amount of Rs. 5.00 lakh has been indicated 
to each of the eligible Central Universities for the purpose of setting up of these Cells. 
 (d) Improvement of quality of higher education is a continuous process.  A substantial increase 
in Plan allocation has been made in the Eleventh Plan  for the expansion of higher education, for setting 
up of institutions such as Cent ral Universities in uncovered States, establishment of National 
Universities aiming for world cla ss standard, Indian Institutes of Technology, Indian Institutes of 
Management, Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research, Indian Institutes of Information 
Technology and Schools for Planning and Architect ure. Expansion of capacity of the existing 
institutions, incentivising State Governments for increasing State outlays on higher education, 
strengthening of science based research in Universiti es, regular updating of curricula, introduction of 
semester system etc., Faculty Improvement Programmes and other reforms have been/are being 
taken up during the Eleventh Plan for improving the quality and relevance of higher education. It has 
also been decided to make National Eligibility Te st (NET) compulsory for appointment as teachers, 
except for those who have obtained Ph.D. degrees  in the relevant disciplines from universities 
following the norms for enrolment, course work and evaluation as may be prescribed by the UGC and 
for those subjects for which NET is not available.  A decision has been taken to improve pay, other 
emoluments and service conditions of  teachers in higher education in order to attract talented persons 
to teaching careers. It has also been decided to create posts of Professors in Under Graduate 
Colleges in order to improve quality of collegiate teaching. 
Appointment of judges to Supreme Court 
 *297. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Supreme Court’s panel, responsi ble for appointments and promotions of judges 
to the Supreme Court, has rejected Government’s ob jections to its latest round of recommendations 
for promotions; 
 (b) the reasons for Government’s refusal and aski ng the Chief Justice of India to reconsider the 
names for elevation; and 
 (c) whether it has escalated the conflict between  Judiciary and the Parliament, and if so, the 
details in this regard? 
 THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R.  BHARDWAJ): (a) to (c) The Judges of the 
High Courts and Supreme Court are appointed according to the pr ocedure laid down in Articles 217 
and 124 respectively of the Constitution of India. In the case of Advocates-on-Record vs. Union of 
India, the Supreme Court interpreted the procedure laid down that the consultation with the Chief 

 25
Justice of India means the co nsultation with the collegium of the Judges which makes 
recommendation for the appointment. According to this interpretation of the Constitution, if the 
Government feels that the recommendation needs to be reconsidered, then it may be referred back to 
the Chief Justice of India for reconsideration. However, if the collegium reiterates the recommendation, 
then the proposal has to be referred to the Pres ident for approval. The same procedure has been 
followed in the latest appointments to the Su preme Court. There is no conflict between the 
Government and the judiciary. However, there have been demands from certain quarters for 
reconsideration of the law laid down in the Advocates-on-Records vs. Union of India.

: (a) to (d) Ministry of Food Processing Industries extends financial assistance in the form of grant-in-

scheme there is provision for interest free loans @ 50% of total cost within earmarked ceilings for

sector to accomplish upcoming demands of processe d dairy products and helping to identify various 
areas of research for future product development,  scalable efficient) technologies and quality 
improvement to revamp the Indian dairy processing sector for domestic as well as export market by 
way of providing financial assistance to the dairy pr ocessing units. MFPI prov ides financial assistance

includes the milk and milk processi ng plants also. The financial assist ance is 25% of the cost of plant

Wastage of fruits and vegetables 
 2173. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether India is the second largest producer  of fruits and vegetabl es in the world, and 25 
per cent of the produce gets damaged because of poor and unscientific storage; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof;  
 (c) the number of cold storages in the country, State-wise; 
 (d) whether each district in the country does not have adequate facility of cold storage and 
exorbitant charges are taken from farmers for using the cold storages; and 
 (e) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken by Government for setting up more cold 
storages in each district in our country? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF FOOD PROCESSI NG INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAI)  
(a) to (e) The level of wastage of agricultural food  items is estimated to be about Rs. 58,000/- crores 
occurring at various stages of handling after harves ting due to fragmented farming, provisions in 
Agricultural Produce Marketing (Development and Re gulation) Act, lack of adequate post-harvest 
infrastructure such as lack of cold chain fac ilities, transportation, proper storage facilities etc. The loss 
due to wastages could be reduced by promoting the development of food processing industries, 
strengthening of post-harvest infr astructure and filling the gaps in the supply chain. However, the 
substantial rate of growth of th e food processing industry from 7% in 2003-04 to 13.14 % in 2006-07 
and the increase in total investment in food pr ocessing sector to Rs. 40,000 crore in 2006-07 has 
contributed to reduction of wastages and better value addition. 
 In order to increase level of processing and to promote food processing industries to exploit both 
the domestic and international ma rket potential for processed food products, Vision 2015 Document 
has been finalized by the Ministry of Food Proces sing Industries (MFPI), which envisages tripling the 
size of the processed food sector by increasing the level of processing of perishables from 6% to 
20% value addition from 20% to 35%  and share in global food trade from 1.5% to 3% by 2015. An 
integrated strategy for promotion of agribusiness -Vision, Strategy and Action Plan for the Food 
Processing Sector has also been approved by the Government. 

 36
 As per the information available with Directorat e of Marketing and Inspection (DMI), Ministry of 
Agriculture, total number of cold storages in the country as on 31.12.2007 is 5316. State-wise and 
capacity-wise details are given in the Statement. (See below) 
 Government does not regulate the charges being levied for utilization of cold storages which are 
generally market driven and dependent upon variou s factors including volume of storage material, 
power supply, fuel cost, labour charges, etc. 
 To encourage setting up of cold chain facilities and backward linkages in the country, Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries (MFPI) has a Plan  Scheme for Cold Chain, Value Addition and 
Preservation Infrastructure during  the 11th Plan to provide financia l assistance to project proposals 
received from public/private orga nizations for cold chain infrastr ucture development. The scheme 
envisages financial assistance in the form of grant-in-aid @ 50% of the total cost of plant and 
machinery and technical civil works in general area s and 75% for North Eastern Region and difficult 
areas subject to a maximum of Rs. 10.00 crore. The initiatives are aimed at filling the gaps in the supply 
chain, strengthening of cold chain infrastructure, establishing value additi on with infrastructural 
facilities like sorting, grading, packaging and proce ssing for horticulture including organic produce, 
marine, dairy, poultry, etc. Other agencies of the Government like National Horticulture Board (NHB), 
Agricultural and Processing Food Products Deve lopment Authority (APEDA), National Cooperative 
Development Corporation (NCDC) and State Governme nt also provide assistance for cold storages 
under their respective schemes.

Scheme under the 10th Five Year Plan with effect  from 31st March, 2007, the Ministry has recently

FPIs in Rajasthan 
 2178. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Mi nister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) the extent of loss suffered due to lack of  cold storage/warehouse/food processing/storage 
facilities in the country, during the last three years, State-wise; 
 (b) the total amount allocated to improve th ese facilities during the period, State-wise; 
 (c) the extent of increase registered in the cap acity of cold storage warehouse/food processing 
in each State; and 
 (d) the steps taken by Government to set up thes e facilities in Rajasthan, during the last three 
years? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF FOOD PROC ESSING INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT 
SAHAI): (a) to (d) According to the Vision 2015 repo rt prepared by Rabo Bank, the level of wastage 
of agricultural food items is es timated to be about Rs. 58,000/- cror es annually, occurring at various 
stages of handling afte r harvesting due to fragmented farming, lack of adequate post-harvest 
infrastructure such as lack of cold chain fac ilities, transportation, proper storage facilities etc. The loss 
due to wastages could be reduced by promoting the development of food processing industries, 
strengthening of post-harvest infrastructure and f illing the gaps in the supply chain. However, the 

 43
substantial rate of growth of th e food processing industry from 7% in 2003-04 to 13.14 % in 2006-07 
and the increase in total investment in food pr ocessing sector to Rs. 40,000 crore in 2006-07 has 
contributed to reduction of wastages and better value addition. Ministry of Food Processing Industries 
does not maintain state specif ic data regarding extent of loss due to lack of cold 
storages/warehouse/food processing/storage facilities. 
 Since financial assistance schemes are project oriented, no funds have been allocated State-
wise. The budget allocation utilized by the Minist ry on infrastructure development including cold 
storages during 2005-06, 2006-07 and 2007-08 was Rs. 15.65 crore, Rs. 13.21 crore and Rs. 14.80 
crore respectively. 
 As per the information available with Directorat e of Marketing and Inspection (DMI), Ministry of 
Agriculture, the capacity of cold storages in the country has been increased from 216.94 lakh MT as on 
31.12.2006 to 233.34 lakh MT as on 31.12.2007 A statem ent indicating State-wise increase in capacity 
of cold storages is enclosed. (See below) 
 To encourage setting up of cold chain facilities and backward linkages in the country, Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries (MFPI) has a Plan  Scheme for Cold Chain, Value Addition and 
Preservation Infrastructure during  the 11th Plan to provide financia l assistance to project proposals 
received from public/private orga nizations for cold chain infrastr ucture development. The scheme 
envisages financial assistance in the form of grant-in-aid @ 50% of the total cost of plant and 
machinery and technical civil works in general area s and 75% for North Eastern Region and difficult 
areas subject to a maximum of Rs. 10.00 crore. The initiatives are aimed at filling the gaps in the supply 
chain, strengthening of cold chain infrastructure, establishing value additi on with infrastructural 
facilities like sorting, grading, packaging and proce ssing for horticulture including organic produce, 
marine, dairy, poultry, etc. Other agencies of the Government like National Horticulture Board (NHB), 
Agricultural and Processing Food Products Deve lopment Authority (APEDA), National Cooperative 
Development Corporation (NCDC) and State Governme nt also provide assistance for cold storages 
under their respective schemes. 
 An increase has been registered in capacity of cold  storages in Rajasthan from 3.12 lakh MT as on 
31.12.2006 to 3.15 lakh MT as on 31.12.2007.’

 †2208. SHRI JAI PRAKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Central Government is considerin g to set up a fund to bring forward the latent 
talents in schools/colleges from which meritorious students may get assistance; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether this fund has actually been set up; 
 (d) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (e) if not, by when this fund is proposed to be set up? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
M.A.A. FATMI): (a) and (b) The Government of India has launched Nati onal Means-cum-Merit 
Scholarship Scheme to award one lakh scholarships every year to meritorious students, whose 
parental income is not more th an Rs. 1,50,000 per annum. The se lected students will be given 
scholarships for study in classes IX to XII. Interest from a corpus of Rs. 3000 crore to be built up over 4 
years, is envisaged to fund the scheme. The firs t installment of Rs. 750 cr ore is proposed to be 
credited to the corpus in 2008-09. 
 (c) to (e) No corpus could be set up due to non- availability of funds. The Ministry of Finance has 
now provided funds to set up corpus under the Sc heme in the first supplem entary grants of the 
Ministry of Human Resource Development but the f unds have not yet been transferred. The corpus 
fund will be set up immediately on availability of funds.

Strategies to meet the requirement 
1. The strategies adopted to meet the requirement are as follows:— 
 i. An enhanced capacity addition programme th rough successive Five Ye ar Plans. During the 
11th Five Year Plan a capacity addition target of 78700 MW ha s been set from  conventional 
energy sources. According to the assessment  of the Central Electricity Authority the 
capacity addition for th e 12th (2012-2017) and the 13th ( 2017-2022) Plan would have to be 
in the range of 90,000 — 95,000 MW and 100, 000 — 105,000 MW respectively. A target of 
15000 MW from new and renewabl e sources has been set for th e 11th Plan and the Ministry 
of New and Renewable Energy has a perspective of further addition of 30,000 MW in the 12th 
and 13th Plan periods. More nuclear reactors are also planned so as to achieve 20,000 MWe 
nuclear power generations by 2020. 
 ii. Development of a number of  Ultra Mega Power Projects of a capacity 4,000 MW each under 
international competitive bidding. 
 iii. Harnessing surplus captive power into the grid. A capacity of 12000 MW of captive  
power is likely to be added to the system du ring Eleventh Plan. Th is could also save  
expenditure on Transmission and Distribution systems as well as associated losses to some 
extent. 
 iv. Development of about 10 ,000 MW capacity through merchant power plant initiative.

country. Preliminary feasibility reports for 162 projects having a total of 48000 MW were 
prepared. 77 projects with a to tal capacity of about 37000 MW wh ich had an expected first 
year tariff less than Rs. 2.50 per unit were se lected for execution. The allocation of these 
projects for execution rests with the host State Government. 
 vi. Development of extensive network of transm ission system commensur ate with the capacity 
addition programme. Addition of new inter-re gional capacities through development of 
National Grid. 
 vii. Energy conservation and energy efficiency through Demand Side Management (DSM) and 
end user initiatives. 
 viii. Rigorous monitoring of capacity addi tion of the on-going generation projects. 
 ix. Renovation, modernization and life extens ion of old and inefficient generation units. 
 x. Power Finance Corporation (PFC) and the Rura l Electrification Corporation (REC) to ensure 
availability of funds so that viable projects are not hampered.

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) As 
envisaged under the provisions of S ection 63 of the Electricity Act, 2 003, the National Electricity Policy 
and the Tariff Policy, the Ministry of Power had i ssued Guidelines for Encouraging Competition in 
Development of Transmission Projects and Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for 
Transmission Services. Under the Guidelines an  Empowered Committee was se t up to facilitate the 
development of private sector pa rticipation through the competitiv e bidding process. The Empowered 
Committee headed by Member, Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) is already in place. 
Standard Bidding Documents as required under th e Guidelines including Request for Qualification 
(RfQ), Request for Proposal (RfP ) and Transmission Service Agreem ent (TSA) have been issued by 
the Ministry. 
 Rural Electrification Corporation (REC) and Power Finance Corporatio n (PFC) have formed 
Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) to coordinate the bid process for procurement of transmission 
services. RfQs for three transmission projects identified by the Empowered Committee for selection of

power from surplus to deficit regions is already in operation. The development of a National Grid is a 
continuous process and its capacity gets enhanced pr ogressively with addition of generation projects

Schemes for energy efficiency 
 2269. SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Mi nister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether eight schemes have been formulat ed by the Ministry for promotion of energy 
efficiency in the country; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c) the expected saving of power in MWs in th e country, with particular  reference to Andhra 
Pradesh? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF  POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) 
The eight schemes formulated for promotion of energy efficiency are:— 
 (1) Bachat Lamp Yojana to promote energy efficient and high quality Compact Fluorescent 
Lamps as replacement for incandescent bulbs in households. 
 (2) Standards  and  Labeling Scheme to lay down minimum energy  performance standards for 
high energy end use equipments  appliances, such as, refrigerators, air-conditioners, tube 
lights, distribution transformers and motors. 
 (3) Energy Conservation Building Code to set minimum energy performance standards for new 
commercial buildings. 
 (4) Agricultural and Municipal Demand Side Management to target replacement of inefficient 
pumpsets, street lighting, etc. 
 (5) Operationalising Energy Conservation Act, 2001 by strengthening the institutional capacity 
of the State Designated Agencies to enable them to perform their regulatory, enforcement 
and facilitative functions in their respective states. 
 (6) Energy Efficiency in Small and Medium Enterprises to target 25 high energy consuming 
clusters to promote energy efficiency through the Ener gy Service Company (ESCO) 
route. 
 (7) Institutional strengthening of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency and other energy efficiency 
institutions to enable them to take up implementa tion of energy effi ciency and energy 
conservation measures. 
 (8) Contribution to the State Energy Conservation Fund as a statutory requirement and to 
provide a matching grant to the fund pari-passu with that of the state Governments. 
 (c) As a result of implementation of these schemes, the targeted avoided capacity during 
Eleventh plan in the country is 10,000 MWs. As  per the Non-convention al Energy Development 
Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Ltd ., the expected saving of power is estimated to be 536.63 MWs in 
the state of Andhra Pradesh.

Electricity losses 
 †2273. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
  DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
 Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that average power loss at national level is estimated to be upto 33 per 
cent; 
 (b) if not, the facts thereof and the amount bein g spent currently on generation of this quantum 
of power; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 133
 (c) whether it is also a fact that most of this lo ss is due to theft and if so, the percentage of the 
theft and whether this power theft is the result  of collusion between Go vernment officials and 
consumers; and 
 (d) if not, the reaction of Government thereto and whether in order to check this theft, the 
Planning Commission has recommended that private se ctor should be entrusted with the responsibility 
of power distribution? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF  POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) 
As per the information furnished by Central Electricit y Authority (CE'A), energy lost in transformation, 
transmission and distribution and energy unaccounted for as a percentage of energy available for 
supply for the country for the year 2007-08 (provision al) is 26.91. Considering the reasonable level of 
losses as 15%, the approximate amount spent on ge nerating the energy lost over and above the 15% 
loss level, the amount works out to be Rs. 16594.21 crore (based on average ra te of power as 197.78 
paisa per unit). 
 (c) Prior to year 2001-02, utilities used to mo nitor Transmission and Di stribution (T and D) 
losses. Concept of Aggregate Tec hnical and Commercial (AT and C) loss was introduced in 2001-02. 
AT and C loss captures not only t echnical losses, but also captures theft, pilferages and commercial 
losses due to poor metering and billing and non-rea lization of dues. The draft report on Performance 
of State Power Utilities for the years 2004-05 to 20 06-07 prepared by the Power Finance Corporation 
indicates that the AT and C Losses of the St ate Power Utilities at the national level for  
2006-07 was 33.07% of the total energy available for sale. 
 (d) The Government had launched the Ac celerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) in the year 2002- 03 with the objective of encourag ing reforms, reducing AT and 
C loss, improving quality of supply of power and im proving consumer satisfaction. The target was to 
reduce AT and C losses to 15% in five years to begin with in urban and high density consumption 
areas. 
 The Central Government has built a national co nsensus to focus on a time bound programme for 
reduction of AT and C losses. In the Chief Minister s' Conference held under the chairmanship of the 
Prime Minister on 28th May 2007, a unani mous resolution was adopted which inter alia included the 
commitment of the States, with appropriate assist ance from the Centre, to establish the necessary 
baseline data and information technology applicat ions for energy accounting and auditing, and for 
ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft. 
 The Government have a pproved the continuation of APDRP wi th some modifications during the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan with revised terms and conditions as a Central Sector Scheme. Power Finance 
Corporation Ltd. (PFC), a Public Sector Undertak ing (PSU) under the Ministry of Power has been 
appointed as the Nodal Agency for operationalising the APDRP in the Eleventh  Plan. The focus of the 
programme during Eleventh Plan is on actual, demonstrable performance in terms of loss reduction. 

 134 
 Planning Commission has not suggested that pr ivate sector should be  entrusted with the 
responsibility of power distribution to check the theft of electricity.

Rajiv Gandhi Kutir Jyoti Yojana 
 2277. SHRI RAMA CHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) what is the percentage of State and the Central Government share under the Rajiv Gandhi 
Kutir Jyoti Yojana; 
 (b) whether it is a fact that this scheme has not been able to achieve the target because of 
negligence of Central public sector which has under taken the work; and 
 (c) whether the State Government have also made such allegations and if so, the details 
thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) Kutir 
Jyoti Programme has been subsumed in the Rajiv  Gandhi Grameen Vidyut ikaran Yojana(RGGVY). 
Under RGGVY 90% capital subsidy of the project cost  is provided by the Central Government and the 
balance 10% is provided by Rural Electrification Co rporation (REC), the nodal agency for RGGVY as 
interest bearing loans to the participating states. Under the scheme, 100% capital subsidy at the rate 
of Rs. 2200/- per connection for un-el ectrified Below Poverty Line (BPL ) households is also provided 
by Central Government as per norms of the erstwhile Kutir Jyoti Programme in all the rural habitations. 
Some of the State Governments on their own choice  have assigned execution of RGGVY works to the 
Central' Public Sector Undertak ings (CPSUs). Out of the 558 RGGVY projects under implementation, 
only 139 projects are being implemented by the CPSUs. 
 (b) The gap between target and achievement is primarily not attributable to the CPSUs which 
have been executing RGGVY works only in 139 ou t of 558 projects being implemented. The main 
reasons attributable to the slow progress under RGGVY are:— 
 • Delay in receipt of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). 
 • Delay in forest clearance. 
 • Delays in land acquisition for 33/11 KV sub-stations. 
 • Limited number of good agencies availa ble for execution of turnkey contracts. 
 • Very high rates quoted by contracting agencies. 
 • Shortage of line material and high prices. 
 • Delays in issuance of road permit and way bills. 
 • Delays in taking over by State Utilitie s of physical assets created by CPSUs. 
 • Delays in issuance of Panchayat Cert ificates for village electrification. 
 • Lack of awareness among village rs for taking new connections. 
 • Very poor upstream rural electric ity infrastructure in some States. 
 • Delay in finalization of BPL lists by some States. 
 • Refusal to waive state and local taxe s on line materials by some states. 
 • Difficult terrain in some states.

 (c) Rural Electrification Corporation (REC), the nodal agency for implementation of RGGVY has 
not received any formal complaint against CPSUs for the slow progress under RGGVY.

T and D losses 
 2281. SHRI N.K. SINGH: Will the Minist er of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) the details of transmission and distribution losses in the power sector during the last three 
years, giving details in terms of quantum as well as percentage of the total generation; 
 (b) the State or town which has recorded heaviest T and D losses; and 
 (c) the steps Government has taken or is taking to reduce T and D losses, for improving the 
viability of power companies? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF  POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) 
Prior to year 2001-02, utilities us ed to monitor Transmission and Distribution (T and D) losses. 
Concept of Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT and C) loss was introduced in 2001-02. AT and 
C loss captures not only technical losses, but also captures theft, pilferages and commercial losses 
due to poor metering and billing an d non-realisation of dues. The draf t report on Performance of State 
Power Utilities for the years 2004-05 to 2006-07 prepar ed by the Power Finance Corporation indicates 
that the AT and C Loss of the State Power Utilitie s at the national level for 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-
07 was 34.82%, 35.18% and 33.07% resp ectively of the total energy available for sale. State-wise 
details are at Statement. (See below) 
 (c) The Government had launched the Ac celerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) in the year 2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms, reducing AT and 

 155
C loss, improving quality of supply of power and im proving consumer satisfaction. The target was to 
reduce AT and C losses to 15% in five years to begin with in urban and high density consumption 
areas. AT and C loss has come down in towns where APDRP has been implemented. Further, some of 
the utilities which adopted various interventions as envisaged under the programme have shown 
significant reduction in AT and C loss. 
 The Central Government has built a national co nsensus to focus on a time bound programme for 
reduction of AT and C losses. In the Chief Minister s' Conference held under the chairmanship of the 
Prime Minister on 28th May 2007, a unani mous resolution was adopted which inter alia included the 
commitment of the States, with appropriate assist ance from the Centre, to establish the necessary 
baseline data and information technology applicat ions for energy accounting and auditing, and for 
ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft. 
 The Government have a pproved the continuation of APDRP du ring the Eleventh Five Year Plan 
with revised terms and conditions as a Central Sector Scheme. The focus of the programme is on 
actual, demonstrable performance in terms of loss  reduction. In the project area, the State Power 
Utilities are expected to achieve Aggregate Techni cal and Commercial (AT and C) loss reduction 
target of 15%. The Utilities are also to achieve the fo llowing target of AT and C loss reduction at utility 
level: 
 • Utilities having AT and C loss ab ove 30%: Reduction by 3% per year 
 • Utilities having AT and C loss be low 30%: Reduction by 1.5% per year 
 Projects under the scheme are to be taken up in Two Parts. Part-A is to include the projects for 
establishment of baseline data and IT applicatio ns for energy accounting/auditing and IT based 
consumer service centers. Part-B includes regular distribution strengthening projects. Scheme also 
contains provision of incentive for utility staff in towns where AT and C loss levels are brought below 
the base line levels.

Power generation capacity 
 2283. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Mini ster of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) the total electricity power generation capacity of India as on date and out of total generation 
capacity, how much is from hydel generation; 
 (b) whether it is a fact that 40 thousand Me ga Watt is to be generated through nuclear deal; 
 (c) if so, how many years it would take to generate to this energy; 
 (d) whether the identified untapped hydel potential is one lakh Mega Watt; and 
 (e) if so, how many, years, it would take to ge nerate hydel energy to the tune of 40 thousand 
Mega Watt since taking the project in hand? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) The 
installed generating capacity (ut ilities) as on 30.11.2008 of the coun try is approximately 1,46,903 MW. 
Out of this, the total Hydro Generating Capaci ty including Small Hydro Projects (included in 
Renewable Energy Sources as on 30.09.2008) is around 38,808 MW. 
 (b) and (c) The Integrated Energy Policy of the country envisages reaching a nuclear power 
capacity of 63,000 MWe by th e year 2031-32. This capacity is planned to be ac hieved through a mix of 
indigenous nuclear reactors and by  setting up atomic parks, 6,000 to 10,000 MWe capacity at a site 
comprising of about 1000 MWe and above nuclear power reactors based on imports. 
 (d) and (e) As per the re-assessment of hydr oelectric potential carried out by CEA (1978-87), 
the hydro potential of the country has been assessed about 1,48,700 MW. Out of this upto 30.11.2008, 
32,931 MW has been developed and 13,085 MW is  under construction leaving 1,02,684 MW as 
untapped. Hydro projects are site specific. Construction period of a 40 MW capacity hydro project 
generally ranges from 4 to 6 years from the date of  placement of orders for main civil works depending 
upon features of the project i.e. type of project (run-of-river or st orage), height of dam, length of 
water conductor system, type of power house (surface or underground), etc.

Loharighat power project in Uttarakhand 
 †2285. SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: 
  SHRI SHREEGOPAL VYAS: 
 Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Bhagirathi would be made to  flow through a tunnel, under the Loharighat 
Project to be built over the river Ganges in Uttarakhand; 
 (b) whether the very existence of the holy Bh agirathi would be in danger due to the same; 
 (c) whether environmentalists have ex pressed serious concerns over it; and 
 (d) whether Government is going to close this hydel power project due to the protest from these 
environmentalists and if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF  POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) 
NTPC is constructing Loharinag Pala Hydro-electric Power Project (4×150 MW) across river Bhagirathi 
in Distt. Uttarkashi of Uttarakhand.  With construction of Barrage at Lo harinag, part of Bhagirathi river 
water is proposed to be diverted through a Head  Race Tunnel and the same shall be released back 
into the river after power generation near Pala. Furt her, eleven perennial stre ams are joining the river 
Bhagirathi within the stretch of about 13.5 km  between Barrage and Power House site. The first 
perennial stream joins at a distance of about 500m from the barrage. Adequate water from the dam is 
also proposed to be released co ntinuously in order to ensure co ntinuous flow. As such the holy 
Bhagirathi River shall not be in danger. 
 (c) and (d) Taking note of the concerns raised  by some NGO’s regarding construction of hydro 
power schemes on the river Ganga,  the NTPC on 18.07.2008, on the direction of the Government, has 
constituted a High Level Expert Group to examine the various issues involved. The Group has been 
granted extension upto 31st December, 2008.

Menace of begging 
 2288. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
  SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: 
 Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware that a surv ey of about 3500 beggars, conducted by Social 
Work Department has revealed that four are degree  holders, six have completed college courses and 
many of them earn around Rs. 500 a day, which is higher than wh at several blue and white collar 
workers make; 
 (b) whether in Delhi alone there are 75,000 beggars; 
 (c) if so, how Government proposes to deal with the growing menace of begging, so that 
educated and literate do not resort to begging; and 
 (d) what is the perspective pl anning to end begging menace? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): (a) A survey on beggary was conducted by 
Department of Social Work, University of Delhi on the request of Government of NCT of Delhi. Out of 
surveyed beggars, 6 were found to be graduates and 4 were post graduates. As per the report, 22 
beggars earn between Rs. 200/- to Rs. 500/- per day. 
 (b) As per above report it is difficult to assess  the exact number of beggars at any given time in

 2296. SHRI AMBETH RAJAN: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) the details of action taken by Govern ment to implement Special Component Plan; 
 (b) whether Government is aware that the spirit of Special Component Plan is thoroughly flouted 
by most State Governments; 
 (c) how Government would impose pe nalty against the defaulting States; 
 (d) whether Government would table a whit e paper on the implementation of Special 
Component Plan during the Tenth Five Year Plan period; 
 (e) what is the agenda in this regard for the current Eleventh Five Year Plan period? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN): (a) Planni ng Commission circulated the consolidated 
guidelines on Scheduled Castes Sub Plan (SCSP) , earlier known as Special Component Plan (SCP), 
in October, 2005, to States/UTs. These guidelines, inter alia, include: 
 • Earmarking of funds under SCSP from the tota l State/UT Plan outlay, at least in proportion 
to SC population. 
 • Placing the earmarked funds under  separate budget head/sub head. 
 • Making the Social Welfare Department/the Department concerned with the welfare of SCs 
as nodal department for implementation of SCSP. 
 • Placing the funds earkarked at th e disposal of the nodal department. 
 (b) and (c) As per the available information, the percentage allocation under SCSP by 
States/UTs has increases from 11.20% in 2005-06, to 12.98% in 2006-07 and 15.82% in 2007-08, as 
against 16.2% share of SCs in total population of  the country. Under the scheme of Special Central 
Assistance to SCSP, 25% of the funds are released to States/UTs on the basis of their performance in 
implementation of SCSP. 
 (d) and (e) Following important measures are en visaged during Eleventh  Five Year Plan for 
effective and meaningful implementation of SCSP. 
 • Development appropriate development program mae, specifically relevant for the overall 
development of SCs. 
 • Designing a special mechanism for form ulation and implementation of  SCSP. 
 • Making actual budgetary provisions through allocation of funds under a special head 
designated for SCSP. 
 • Ensuring timely release of SCSP funds for the purpose (s) they are meant for.

Legal and financial assistance to women 
 2303. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Mini ster of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government has decided to provide legal and financial assistance to women who 
have been deserted by their NRI husbands in fore ign countries and ensure their rehabilitation and 
repatriation; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether the Ministry had a discussion with the Ministry of Overseas  Affairs on the subject; 
and 
 (d) if so, the further reaction of both the Ministries on the subject? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINI STRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) Yes, Si r. The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs 
had introduced a scheme to provide legal/financia l assistance to Indian women deserted by their 
overseas Indian spouses. The assistance will be provided to Indian wo men who are victims of 
fraudulent marriages and deserted by their ov erseas Indian husbands or are facing divorce 
proceedings in a foreign country. The scheme has been launched in USA, UK, Australia, New Zealand 
and Gulf where several such cases are being reported. 
 (c) and (d) Yes, Sir. A Ministerial Sub-Committe e under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Ministry 
of Overseas Indian Affairs and ha ving representatives from various central Ministries  including the 
Ministry of Women and Child Development and St ate Governments was constituted to study the 
problems faced by Indian women deserted by  their overseas Indian spouses and give 
recommendations. The important recommendations of the sub-committee are as under:- 
 • All marriages solemnized in India should be compulsorily registered. 

 201
 • Litigations related to NRI marriages sh ould be taken up in fast track Courts. 
 • Whenever there is an ongoing litigation in a fo reign court, the Indian bride’s case should not 
go un-represented. 
 • A vigorous information campaign may be launc hed to educate prospective brides and their 
families to take possib le precautions before entering in to marriage alliance with overseas 
Indians. 
 • States/Union Territories should pass on inform ation regarding Court Or ders against NRIs to 
Emigration Authorities to prevent such people from leaving India against these orders. 
 • Bilateral agreements may be signed with foreign countries to protect the victims of NRI 
marriages.

 The object of the proposed legisl ation is to establish a world-clas s institution that will attract the 
brightest and the most dedicated students and teachers from across South Asia with a view to: 
 (a) Disseminating and advanc ing knowledge, wisdom and understanding by providing 
instructional and research facilities in various branches of learning. 
 (b) Taking appropriate measures for promotin g innovations in teaching-learning process. 
 (c) Promoting regional peace an d security by creating a multicultural atmosphere of tolerance 
and understanding. 
 (d) Fostering sound civic sense and to train th em to become useful citizens of democratic 
societies.

norms in teaching, research and curriculum that are acceptable to all member states of the SAARC.

centres and specialized laboratories and such other units for research and instruction as are necessary 
for the furtherance of its objects,  to institute Chairs, principalshi ps, professorships, readerships and 
lectureships and other teaching an d academic positions, required by the University and to appoint 
persons to such chairs, principa lships, etc., and other teaching and academic positions and to 
establish and maintain campuses, centres and Regional Centres. ...(Interruptions)...

 (i) The University will be the first International University to be hosted by India in Delhi.

Scarcity of water 
 †*308. SHRI BRIJ BHUSHAN TIWARI: 
  SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
 Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware of scarcity of water in the country; 
 (b) if so, whether any initiative is being taken by Government for the distribution of water of 
Chenab, Kosi and Brahmaputra rivers under the international law; and 
 (c) if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES  
(SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) the UNESCO Water Portal states that water 
scarcity has been defined as a situation where wate r availability in a country or a region is below 
1000 cubic metre per person per year. Considering the population of 2001 census, the per capita 
water availability in India works out to be 1820 Cu bic Metre. The per capita water availability is 
declining because of populati on growth. The National Commission on Integrated Water 
Resources Development has estimated that by the year 2050, when the population is expected 
to stabilize, the per capita water availability would be 1140 Cubic Metre. However, the per capita 
water availability varies considerably from one basin to another. 
 (b) and (c) Distribution of Chenab waters is  governed by the provisions of Indus Waters 
Treaty 1960 between India and Pakistan. Under the Treaty, India is under obligation to let flow all 
the Chenab waters and not permit any interfer ence with these waters, except for uses, as 
specified in the Treaty. A bilateral agreemen t on Kosi Barrage was signed between the 
Governments of India and Nepal in 1954, which wa s later revised in December 1966. There is no 
bilateral agreement with China for distribution of waters of Brahmaputra river. However, a Joint 
Expert Level Mechanism (ELM) has been set up under cooperation with China for cooperation

 *309. MS. SUSHILA TIRIYA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that there is a like lihood that lakhs of employees may have to lose 
their jobs in the near future in view of the global economic crisis; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c) the steps taken by Government in this regard? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) Unlike the developed countries where job losses have been reported  
due to the global financial crisis, the impact has been limited in India as a large proportion  
of population is employed in the agriculture sector which has  not been  affected by the  crisis.  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 11 
Besides, the services sector with a large share in  GDP has also been less affected. Even in the 
export sector which registered negative growth in October, 2008, the fall was mainly due to a 
spike in export growth in October, 2007 and is limited to some sectors only. While no 
comprehensive surveys have been conducted to estimate the likely job losses in India due to 
global economic crisis, a sample study of 121 export related companies (for the period  
August-October, 2008) by Department of Commerce  has indicated fall in jobs due to slowdown 
in some export sectors. A recent FICCI survey  indicates some downsizing in employment in 
coming months particularly in some export se ctors. Meanwhile, GDP growth is expected to 
moderate somewhat from very high growth rate in  the last 3 years, yet remain sufficiently high 
this year generating new employment opportunities. 
 (c) Government is concerned about the possible  impact of global financial crisis on the 
Indian economy, including employment, and severa l measures, financial and fiscal, have been 
taken. RBI’s measures to enhance liquidity in the market and the Government’s fiscal stimulus to 
help industrial growth and empolyment like reduct ion in three major ad valorem rates of Central 
Excise duty applicable to non-petroleum products  by 4 percentage points, withdrawai of export 
duty on iron ore (fines) and additional plan expenditure of upto Rs 20,000 crore in the current 
year would help address the problem. Further.  3.24 crore households have been provided 
employment under National Rural Employment Guarantee Act as on 15.12.2008 in the current 
financial year. 
Annual growth rate 
 †*310. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
  DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
 Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that according to the mid term annual report of the Reserve Bank of 
India (RBI), the annual growth rate  in the current year is expected to be 7.5 per cent to 8 per 
cent and according to the Central Bank, the price index is expected to rise upto 7 per cent in the 
current year; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether on the basis of the above figures, the growth rate in the country can be said to 
be satisfactory to the common man; and 
 (d) if not, what is Government’s reaction thereto? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) The Reserv e Bank of India (RBI) has revised their GDP forecast for 
2008-09 to a range of 7.5-8.0 per cent. The growth has been revised downwards in view of the 
fact that the global down turn may be deeper and more protracted than expected earlier, with 
consequent adverse implication through trade and financial channels for emerging economies, 
including India, getting amplified. This could have  effects in the form of potential terms of Trade 
losses, erosion of export competitiveness and restricted external financing causing the growth in 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 12
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at factor cost co nstant prices to decelerate to 7.8 per cent 
during April-September (2008-09) as against the growth of 9.3 per cent in the corresponding 
period of 2007-08. 
 The RBI in their Mid-Term Review of Annual Policy for the year 2008-09 have maintained 
their projection made during the Annual Policy Review in April 2008, for inflation at 7 percent by 
end March 2009, keeping in view the supply ma nagement measures taken by the Government 
and the lagged demand response to the monetary policy measures taken by the RBI over the 
last one year. RBI’s endeavour is to bring down inflation to a tolerable level of below 5 per cent at 
the earliest, while aiming for convergence with the global average inflation of around 3.0 per cent 
over the medium term. 
 (c) and (d) Though growth rate of between 7 to 8 per cent represents some slow down 
from the high average growth of around 8.8 per cent in the last five years, this should be seen in 
the context that in the previous six-years (1997-98 to 2002-03) there was not even one year in 
which growth exceeded 7 per cent. 
 The growth in the first half of 2008-09 is ch aracterized by an increase in the ratio of 
Government Consumption Expenditure component in the demand side of GDP, emanating from 
enhanced public expenditure directed towards promoting improved access to essential services, 
infrastructure development and rural prosperity aimed towards inclusive growth which impact the 
common man.

Impact of global economic recession 
 †*320. SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that India is also affected by global economic recession; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether Government has formulated any scheme or set up any Commission to assess 
the effects of this economic recession; 
 (d) if so, the effects of the recessi on on different sectors so far; and 
 (e) if not, the manner in which Government would assess the fallout of this recession? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) The Glob al economic recession has impacted the domestic economy. 
As per the estimates released by the Central Statis tical Organisation of Ministry of Statistics and 
Programme Implementation, the growth rate of  the economy, measured in terms of Gross 
Domestic Product at factor cost, was 7.8 per cent in the first half (April-September) of the 
financial year 2008-09 as against the growth of 9.3 percent in the first half of 2007-08. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 32
 The growth in the first half of 2008-09 for agri culture, industry and services are estimated at 
2.9 per cent, 6.5 per cent and 9.8 per cent as compared to 4.5 per cent. 9.3 per cent and 10.7 
per cent in the corresponding period of 2007-08. There are signs of slowdown in growth across 
different sectors. 
 The global slowdown has its implications on the domestic economy, primarily through the 
moderation in capital flows, the financial markets and trade. The impact of the global crisis on 
the domestic economy has been largely transmitte d directly through the Indian equity and the 
foreign exchange markets and through trade channels and indirectly through the money, debt 
and credit markets. While exact effects of the global slowdown are difficult to quantify 
because the complexity of the crisis and spreading effects in the international economy, it is 
expected that there may be some moderation in India’s capital flows and in the growth of 
exports. 
 (c) to (e) The Government has not set up any Commission to assess the impact of the 
global economic recession. The Government monitors  and evaluates, from time to time, at the 
highest official and political levels the effect of global economic develo pments on the Indian 
economy in formulating its economic policies and designs counter cyclical steps accordingly. To 
safeguard the economy against adverse impact of the global financial crisis, the Reserve Bank of 
India has taken measures, ‘Inter alia’, for reduction in Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity 
Ratio, reduction in repo and reverse repo rates and for liberalising access to external commercial 
borrowings. The Government has announced a fi scal package which includes additional plan 
expenditure, reduction in the ‘ad valorem’ Cenvat rate and measures to support exports. These 
measures have ensured the effective functionin g of the financial system and improvement in 
liquidity in the money market and provide stimulus to the economy to counter the slowdown in 
growth.

Mandatory air safety management 
 2327. MS. MABEL REBELLO: 
  SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
 Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether there is a proposal to set up a new body to ensure and maintain air safety; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether it is also proposed to work out a mandatory safety management system, for all 
airlines for the purpose; 
 (d) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (e) what are the details of strides that have si nce been made by India in ensuring air safety 
since mid-air horrific collision at Charkhi-Dadri in Haryana in 1997? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): 
(a) and (b) No such proposal is under active co nsideration in the Ministry of Civil Aviation. 

 34
However, it has been decided to move in the dir ection of separation of investigation wing from 
the regulatory wing as recommended by the Inte rnational Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). 
DGCA has been requested to prepare a roadmap for the same. 
 (c) and (d) Air Traffic Service Provider and the licensed aerodrome holders are required to 
establish Safety Management System (SMS). SMS has also been introduced for air operators 
and maintenance organizations which would be come effective from January 2009. It is a 
systematic approach to manage safety with established lines of safety accountability throughout 
the organization starting from the very top. 
 (e) After mid-air collision on 12.11.96 at Char khi Dardri, Haryana, various safety measures 
have been taken which include in stallation of air-borne Collision Avoidance System, installation 
of Transponder (A,C and S Type), Minimum Safe  Altitude Warning System, installation of 
Monopulse Secondary Surveillance Radars (M SSRs), introduction of Crew Resource 
Management Programme as integral part of crew training, introduction of proficiency check for 
English language for pilots, bifurcation of AT S Route G-452 into arrival/departure corridors 
within the limits of Delhi Terminal Area, laying the requirements for the minimum parameters to 
be recorded on DFDR/FDR, introduction of a scheme for licensing of controllers etc.

establishment; 

 39

expatriates whose security clearance had not been done by agencies; and

violations?

PATEL): (a) and (b) No foreign registered aircraft is allowed to operate to/from and within

 (i) High antiquity of its early texts/recorded history over a period of 1500-2000 years.

 (iii) The literacy tradition be original and not borrowed from another speech community.

Futures Trading Policy 
 2365. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the futures trading policy of Gove rnment has resulted in extreme inflation and 
has encouraged the practice of speculation to a greater extent; 
 (b) whether it is a fact that billions of Indian  currency is going abroad leading to hike in 
most of the commodities as a result thereof; 
 (c) whether Government would consider imposing ban on futures, trading in order to 
check inflation; 
 (d) if so, by when; and 
 (e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 66
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) The Expert Committee chaired by Professor Abhijit Sen, Member, Planning 
Commission, constituted by the Government in  March, 2007 to study the impact of futures 
trading on the prices of agricult ural commodities has stated that in view of conflicting results 
from daily, as against weekly and monthly data, no strong conclusion can be drawn on whether 
introduction of futures trade is associated with d ecrease or increase in spot price volatility. The 
Expert Committee also analyzed an nual growth rate in prices of sensitive commodities (food 
grains and sugar) in pre-future period and post future period and concluded that although 
inflation clearly increased post-futures in some se nsitive commodities that have higher weight in 
consumer price indices, it is not possible to ma ke any general claim that inflation accelerated 
more in commodities with futures trading. As on December 6, 2008, the inflation rate measured 
by the Wholesale Price Index stood at 6.84 percent, compared to 12.91 percent on  
August 2, 2008. 
 (b) Futures trading in commodities in India does  not appear to lead to any flight of Indian 
currency abroad. 
 (c) to (e) As a matter of caution, the Fo rward Markets Commission (FMC) had suspended 
futures trading in tur, urad, wheat and rice in 2007. Subsequently, the FMC had suspended 
futures trading in chana, soy oil, potato and rubber w.e.f. 7.05.08, which was not extended 
beyond 30.11.08. Since the Abhijit Sen Committee could not establish any definite causal 
relationship between futures tradin g and rice in prices of commodities there is no proposal to 
ban futures trading in more commodities.

Benefits of loan waiver scheme 
 2369. SHRI PRAKASH JAVADEKAR: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that more than 60 million farmers out of total farming community of 
India have not received any benefit of loan waiver scheme declared by Government; 
 (b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
 (c) how does Government propose to extend th e benefits of the loan waiver scheme to the 
farmers who have not been benefited in the present scheme? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) Government of India has implemented Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt 
Relief (ADWDR) Scheme, 2008, which covered all direct agricultural loans extended to ‘marginal 
and small farmers’ and ‘other farmers’  by Scheduled Commercial Banks, Regional Rural Banks, 
Cooperative Credit Institutions (including Urban Cooperative Banks) and Local Area Banks that 
were disbursed during the period from April 1, 1997 to March 31, 2007, were overdue on 
December 31, 2007 and that remained unpaid until February 29, 2008. In the case of small  
or marginal farmer, the entire ‘eligible amount’ was waived while in the case of ‘other farmers’, 

 69
there is a One Time Settlement (OTS) Scheme under which the farmer is to be given a rebate of 
25% of the ‘eligible amount’ subject to the condition that the farmer pays the balance of 75% of 
the ‘eligible amount’. 
 As per the provisional figures, a total of 3.01 crore small and marginal farmers and 0.67 
crore ‘other farmers’ have benefitted from the Sc heme involving debt waiver and debt relief of 
Rs. 65,318.33 crore. 
 (c) The prime objective of the ADWDR Scheme was to cover all those farmers who, for 
some reason or the other, could not pay back th eir overdues to the banks and therefore, were 
under continued indebtedness. Such farmers, as a result, could not borrow from the banking 
system. ADWDR Scheme was designed to de-clog this line of credit and help such needy 
farmers, making them eligible for fresh credit in the process. 
 As provided in the Guidelines of ADWDRS, every lending institution has appointed one or 
more Grievance Redressal Officers (GROs) for ea ch State (having regard to the number of 
branches in that State). The name and address of the GRO concerned have been displayed in 
each branch of the lending institution. The GRO has the authority to receive representations from 
aggrieved farmers and pass appropriate orders thereon.

 75
 (b) The following steps have been taken by  the Government to improve the direct and 
indirect tax revenues: 
 (I) Direct Taxes  
  1. Monitoring of advance tax payment of top tax payers. 
  2. Emphasis on collection out of arrear demand and monitoring of the cases of top 
defaulters. 
  3. Selection of cases under scrutiny based on objective financial parameters.  
  4. Computerization of the Departmental business processes and data bases for
